n03_1: 1. what is a large language model (llm)? definition a large language model is an ai model trained on huge amounts of text that can understand and generate human language. it is the engine behind chatgpt, claude and gemini. l arge: billions of parameters, trained on a huge amount of text l anguage: reads and writes human language m odel: a program that learned from data, not from written rules fun fact: training gpt-4 cost openai more than $100 million (₹800+ crore), as ceo sam altman said in 2023. 2. how an llm thinks predicts prompt: "the capital of india is ..." goes into the llm (a transformer neural network), which gives a probability for every token in its vocabulary. the capital of india is → llm transformer neural network → probability for every token in the vocabulary new 81% delhi 15% mumbai 1% others <1% it guesses, it doesn't "know" every possible next word gets a probability. the model picks one from the top. it learned by itself it read huge amounts of text and kept guessing the next word. no one labelled the data. a new answer each time because it picks from probabilities, the reply can change every time you ask. 3. what are parameters? definition parameters are the weights and biases inside a model. they are numbers the model learns during training, and together they store everything it knows. "8b" means 8 billion of them. weights decide how much each input matters. biases shift the result up or down. number of parameters (b = billion) gpt-2 1.5b llama 3 · small 8b llama 3 · medium 70b gpt-3 175b llama 3 · large 405b gpt-4, claude and gemini: not disclosed bigger is smarter: more parameters usually means a more capable model. 4. what is a token? definition a token is the small piece of text an llm reads and writes. it can be a whole word, part of a word, or a symbol. the model never sees letters or words, only the number (id) of each token. text i am learning langchain ↓ split into tokens tokens i  am  learning  lang chain ↓ each token has a fixed id token ids 40 939 7524 27830 20848 why do we need tokens? computers only work with numbers, so text has to become numbers first. letters would make every text very long. whole words would need a huge vocabulary and would break on new words. tokens are the middle way. cost, speed and the context window are all counted in tokens. rule of thumb: 1 \text{ token} \approx 0.75 \text{ words} (about 4 characters in english). try it yourself at platform.openai.com/tokenizer . every company has its own tokenizer (its own algorithm and vocabulary), so the same text can become different tokens and ids in different models. recap: what happens after the id? each id is looked up in a table and becomes a list of numbers (an embedding). the transformer works on these numbers and gives a score to every token in the vocabulary. the scores become the probabilities you saw above, and the model picks the next token. vocabulary size is the number of different tokens a model knows. gpt-2 had about 50k (50,257). llama 3 has about 128k, and newer models go higher. what about other languages? the vocabulary is shared by all languages, so there is no separate english vocabulary. languages like hindi get fewer whole-word tokens, so the same sentence breaks into more pieces. that costs more tokens and fills the context window faster.

n07_1: 1. what is a prompt? definition a prompt is the input you give to a large language model to get the response you want. weak prompt "tell me about tokens." no clear task no context: who is asking? no format: the answer can be any length → strong prompt explain what a token is to a student who already knows python in 2 lines, with one example. instruction what to do context what it needs to know format how the answer should look 2. the system prompt definition a system prompt is an instruction you give the model before the conversation . it sets the model's role, behaviour and rules . every production chatbot, from a finance assistant to a health bot or a support agent , is configured with a system prompt first. real products stack more layers on top, and we build those later. at its core, a system prompt fixes the model's role , its behaviour and its rules . a strong one spells out five things, and you add only the ones your app needs. one system prompt from a finance chatbot, split into its parts role you are a personal finance chatbot. tone be polite and use simple language. task help users make a monthly budget. limits give no stock advice. answer only finance questions. format use a maximum of 3 bullet points. 3. three types of messages the system prompt is sent as a message. in fact, the model does not get one plain string. it gets a list of messages, and each message has a role. you send system and human messages. the model sends back an ai message. system message "answer in one word." rules for the model. written by you, the developer. systemmessage human message "capital of rajasthan?" the question. it comes from the user. humanmessage you send → llm reads the messages replies → ai message "jaipur" the reply from the model. aimessage system sets the rules. human asks. ai answers.

why do we need ann? searching a few thousand vectors is easy. searching millions is the problem. here is the story. the issue a company stores 1 million chunks. a user asks a question, and we must find the few best chunks, fast. the first try score the question against every vector, then sort. this is called brute force . it is exact: it always finds the true best chunks. why it fails one question costs 1 million scores. each score multiplies 1,536 pairs of numbers, so one question needs about 1.5 billion multiplications. ten times more chunks means ten times more work, written o(n) . and it is paid on every question . the fix do not score everything. look only in the places where the best chunks are likely to be. once in a while we may miss the true best one, but the search becomes many times faster. this is ann . how the work grows with the number of vectors, for one question. vectors stored (n) multiplications for one question (n × 1,536) feeling 10,000 15,360,000 a moment 1,000,000 1,536,000,000 slow 100,000,000 153,600,000,000 far too slow big o: the work grows in a straight line with n. this is called flat or brute-force search, and written o(n × d). it is exact, but it is paid on every question . d = 1,536 is the size of an openai small embedding. what is ann? ann stands for approximate nearest neighbor . let us break the name into its words. nearest neighbor the stored vector that is closest to the question. we want the k nearest ones. approximate we accept “very close” instead of “guaranteed the closest”. rarely, the true best chunk is missed. what we get a big gain in speed, for a tiny loss in accuracy. exact search compare with every vector. always finds the true closest ones. slow on big data. approximate search look at a small part of the vectors, chosen cleverly. very fast. might miss a true neighbour now and then. recall tells you how good an ann index is: of the true top 10, how many did it find? a recall of 0.95 means 9 or 10 of them. you can trade speed for recall with the index settings. what ann is a shortcut that chooses which vectors to score, so we do not score all of them. what it is not a new way to score. we still score with cosine, dot product or euclidean. the flow ann picks a small set of candidates. the score ranks them. the top-k come back. the families of ann algorithms there are dozens of ann algorithms. you do not need to learn them all. they fall into five families , and each family uses one main trick. family the trick a picture algorithms groups sort the vectors into groups. search only the nearest groups. books sorted into sections ivf graphs link each vector to its neighbours. walk from link to link toward the question. a road network hnsw, diskann compression store a smaller copy of each vector, so more fit in memory and scoring is faster. a short summary instead of the whole book pq, scann (scann also uses groups) hashing give similar vectors the same label. search only the matching label. same postcode, same area lsh trees cut the space in two, again and again, like a game of twenty questions. twenty questions annoy we explain three in detail: ivf (groups), hnsw
